properties.title: Washburn Park Water Tower
properties.architect: Harry Wild Jones; sculptural figures by John K. Daniels
properties.blurb: A stone lantern on the ridge — eight guardians holding the sky. Built as working water infrastructure; now a neighborhood landmark that still feels like covered old tech.

story.hook: Eight figures keep watch from the ridge.
story.body: In 1893 the Washburn Park Water Tower rose above Tangletown’s tangle of streets. Harry Wild Jones designed a working reservoir dressed as a medieval keep; sculptor John K. Daniels gave it eight guardians — knights of civic water. The pumps are quiet now, but the tower still reads like a piece of lost city machinery left standing in plain sight.
story.wonder: What other towers once threaded water, light, or signal through the ridge — and what still hides under renovations?

then.label: Then · 1893
then.caption: Working water tower: reservoir, pumps, and a skyline statement for Washburn Park.

now.label: Now · 2026
now.caption: Landmark and neighborhood icon. Infrastructure retired; the form remains.

properties.title: Justice Page / Washburn High
properties.dates: Campus era layered; Washburn High opened 1925; Justice Page (formerly Ramsey) on the same ridge block
properties.blurb: Two school houses on one ridge — and a whispered older care. Local lore points toward a possible Washburn orphan asylum thread under the modern campus story.

story.hook: Where classrooms stand, older care may have stood.
story.body: Justice Page Middle School and Washburn High share the Tangletown ridge along West 49th. The buildings you see are school architecture of the twentieth century — but neighbors pass down a softer question: did a Washburn orphan asylum once claim ground near here? The map marks the cluster as altered ground: surviving institutions on possibly older social footprint. Contested memory stays quiet until you ask.
story.wonder: If an asylum stood nearby, what traces remain in plats, photographs, or family stories — and what was paved over?

properties.title: St. John's Lutheran Church
properties.dates: Neighborhood congregation on Nicollet, just north of Justice Page
properties.blurb: A pinnacle on Nicollet, a short walk north of the school ridge. Neighbor lore whispers of tunnels — passages that may or may not have linked church and campus underground.

story.hook: North of the schools, a steeple and a rumor.
story.body: St. John’s Lutheran sits on Nicollet Avenue, just north of Justice Page. In Tangletown walks, people still trade the tunnel story: a passage under the ridge, connecting sacred ground to school ground — escape route, utility trench, or pure neighborhood myth. The map doesn’t prove the tunnel. It invites you to stand here and wonder what the ground remembers.
story.wonder: If a tunnel existed, where would its mouths be — and what else travels under Tangletown’s tangle?

then.label: Then · rumor layer
then.caption: Placeholder for tunnel lore: possible underground link toward the school ridge.

now.label: Now · street face
now.caption: Active church on Nicollet. The tunnel remains an open neighborhood question.
